June 2018 Steven and I hiked the Arctic Circle Trail, Greenland's most popular backpacking trail, around 100 miles of spectacular scenery including tons of lakes and fjords, waterfalls, towering snow-covered mountains, and sweeping views!  

Difficulties encountered: 
Arranging for trailhead transportation (if you wish to skip the 10-mile pre-trail road portion between Kangerlussuaq and Kellyville), being prepared for severe weather conditions (including heavy rain, intense cold, strong winds, white-out fog, and snowstorms even in the summer), dealing with the nonstop assault of mosquitoes, avoiding unsafe encounters with wildlife, hiking through challenging bogs and wetlands (wet feet for days), and safely carrying out river crossings (which also means not crossing when river levels are too high). 

More info about the hike can be found here:

Greenland, the world's largest island, offers a breathtaking blend of stark, icy landscapes and vibrant, culturally rich communities. Ilulissat, located on Disko Bay, is famed for the Ilulissat Icefjord, a UNESCO World Heritage Site where colossal icebergs calve from the Sermeq Kujalleq glacier. This spectacular natural wonder is a gateway to experiencing the raw power of Greenland's ice.

Nearby, Disko Bay is a haven for whale watching and exploring the Arctic waters. Qeqertarsuaq, on Disko Island, features dramatic volcanic landscapes and lush valleys, offering a stark contrast to Greenland's icy environment. The town itself is charming, with colorful houses and a rich history tied to Norse settlers.

Embarking on a cruise down Greenland's west coast reveals stunning vistas of towering icebergs, rugged coastlines, and remote settlements. This journey provides a unique perspective on the island's vast and varied terrain, with opportunities to see diverse wildlife and visit traditional Inuit communities.

Nuuk, the capital, blends modernity with tradition. The city boasts museums, such as the Greenland National Museum, which houses a wealth of artifacts and exhibits on Greenlandic culture and history. Nuuk's vibrant arts scene and culinary offerings make it a fitting end to an unforgettable Arctic adventure.

Groenlandia (en groenlandés: Kalaallit Nunaat, ‘tierra de los kalaallits’, y en danés: Grønland, ‘tierra verde’)​ es una isla en la zona nororiental de América del Norte, entre los océanos Atlántico y Glacial Ártico, que políticamente es una nación constituyente del Reino de Dinamarca. Con un total de 2 166 086 km² (81 % cubiertos de hielo), se considera la isla más grande del mundo, tomando la definición de Australia como masa continental. Su capital y ciudad más poblada es Nuuk (en danés: Godthåb). Durante más de un milenio Groenlandia ha estado asociada cultural y políticamente con Europa Septentrional (en concreto con Escandinavia).

Los primeros habitantes de Groenlandia fueron los llamados esquimales. La prehistoria de Groenlandia es una historia de repetidas olas de inmigración paleoesquimal o inuit provenientes de las islas al norte de Norteamérica. Siendo uno de los lugares geográficos más extremos de la extensión cultural de estos pueblos, sus vidas se encontraban en constante peligro y las culturas nacieron y murieron con el paso de los siglos.

Greenland (Greenlandic: Kalaallit Nunaat, "land of the Kalaallits," Danish: Grønland, "green land") is an island in northeastern North America, between the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, and is politically a constituent nation of the Kingdom of Denmark. With a total area of ​​2,166,086 km² (81% covered by ice), it is considered the world's largest island, assuming Australia is defined as a landmass. Its capital and most populous city is Nuuk (Danish: Godthåb). For over a millennium, Greenland has been culturally and politically associated with Northern Europe (specifically Scandinavia).

The first inhabitants of Greenland were the Inuit. Greenland's prehistory is a story of repeated waves of Paleo-Inuit migration from the islands north of North America. Being one of the most extreme geographical locations in the cultural reach of these peoples, their lives were in constant danger and cultures were born and died over the centuries.

In February I travelled to Greenland to photograph the aurora and it's ice fjords with Ollie Taylor Photography.

What I didn’t expect was how much the experience would test patience, resilience, and perspective.

Over 18 days I walked more than 123 km across frozen fjords, boardwalks, and Arctic trails, climbing over 3,100 metres in snow and ice, often in temperatures below -20°C and wind chills reaching -44°C.

There were flight cancellations, whiteouts, frozen camera gear, and long nights out in the freezing cold. My fingers are still feeling it.

And then the sky would erupt.

One of the most unexpected signals came not from the sky, but from the ground — the Greenland sled dogs would begin to howl before the aurora appeared. Again and again, the pattern repeated: the dogs first, then the light.

This film is a collection of those moments:
 • Ice cracking beneath frozen lakes
 • Helicopter flights between the remote Arctic towns of Qaarsut and Uummunnaq
 • Wind whipping snow across the Ilulissat tundra
 • The red sunrise over Uummannaq
 • And ten aurora displays across Ilulissat and Uummannaq

Greenland is not a place you simply visit.
It’s a place you move through, adapt to, and learn from.

If there was one lesson the Arctic taught me, it was this:

A weather and an aurora forecast can often looking bad.
Sometimes nothing happens for a long time.
Sometimes you have to go back out into the cold.

But if you're willing, you’re patient, the clouds part and the sky opens.
